subject_entity.title_display: Epistula 64 (Letter to Fidus on Infant Baptism)
subject_entity.notes: Cyprian's letter c. 252 to Bishop Fidus in response to the question of whether baptism should be delayed until the eighth day after birth (by analogy with circumcision); the Council of Carthage 252 unanimously ruled that baptism should not be delayed — infants may be baptized as early as the second or third day; key witness for the assumption of infant baptism as standard practice and the council's reasoning that God's grace should not be withheld from any soul.

object_entity.notes: Major North African city; center of Latin Christianity from Tertullian through Cyprian and Augustine; seat of important regional councils.

evidence.notes: The letter reports a council ruling at Carthage.

passage.excerpt: Paraphrase: But in respect of the case of infants, which you say ought not to be baptized within the second or third day after their birth, and that the old law of circumcision should be regarded, so that you think one who is just born should not be baptized and sanctified within the eighth day — we all thought very differently in our council. For in this course which you thought was to be taken, no one agreed; but we all rather judged that the mercy and grace of God ought to be denied to no man born.
passage.notes: Council of Carthage 252 ruling: infant baptism not to be delayed; grace denied to none

subject_entity.notes: Gnostic teacher; studied in Alexandria, later prominent in Rome c. 138–160. Founded Valentinianism, the most influential Gnostic school, teaching a complex pleroma of divine emanations (Aeons) and a demiurge subordinate to the supreme God. Opposed apostolic succession, bodily resurrection, and the authority of the OT.

object_entity.proposition_label: Faith is transmitted through apostolic succession
object_entity.description: The bishops who succeed the apostles are authoritative guarantors of the received tradition.

evidence.notes: Valentinus claimed private secret knowledge transmitted from Theudas (disciple of Paul) — bypassing apostolic succession.

passage.excerpt: Valentinus adapted the principles of the heretical school called Gnostic to his own peculiar character of school. He affirmed that in the invisible and ineffable heights there exists a perfect, pre-existent Aeon — Proarche, Propator, and Bythus — invisible and incomprehensible. With him was also Ennoia, whom he calls Charis and Sige. This Bythus, at last resolving to send forth from himself the beginning of all things, deposited this production as a seed in the womb of Sige. The result was Nous and Aletheia — the beginning of a vast pleroma of divine emanations.

source.title: Against Heresies
source.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
source.notes: Five-book refutation of Gnosticism; ANF Vol. 1 translation by Roberts and Rambaut, revised for New Advent by Kevin Knight.
